chapters.summary: Chair Lincoln Restler introduces himself and thanks committee counsel Alex Polinoff, policy analyst Alex Yablon, financial analyst Andrew Lane Lawless, and chief of staff Molly Haley. He sets up the oversight hearing on the city's minority and women-owned business program.
chapters.title: Chair Restler opens hearing and thanks committee staff

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Sergeant.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: My name is Lincoln Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I have the privilege of chairing the Committee on Contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And usually at the end of my opening remarks, I thank the staff, but I just wanted to actually do that at the beginning because

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's important.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We are fortunate to have a truly expert committee counsel in Alex Polinoff, so thank you so much for just providing such helpful guidance to us as the relatively new chair of this committee.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I want to also thank our policy analyst, Alex Yablon, and the principal financial analyst, newly to this committee, Andrew Lane Lawless.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you all for your hard work.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I especially want to thank my chief of staff, Molly Haley, who is brilliant.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And all of the smart things that are said today are a result of her and all of the mistakes are a result of me.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I'll begin with my opening.

chapters.summary: Restler traces the MWBE program from 1989 through its halt under Mayor Giuliani and reestablishment in 2005. He notes two decades of small purchase programs, mentorship, and agency goals but says much remains to be done.
chapters.title: Restler recounts history of NYC MWBE program

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're having an oversight hearing on the city's minority and women-owned business program.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: New York City first developed an MWB program back in 1989, and after a review of the city's contracts, found that MWEs were substantially underutilized.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the program was halted by Mayor Giuliani, one of his many failures, but the city council reestablished the program back in 2005.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And over the past 20 years, we have made significant strides in opening up opportunities for MWBEs in city contracting through small purchase programs, mentorship, and ambitious agency goals.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But much more remains to be done.

chapters.summary: Restler highlights the Comptroller's annual MWBE report showing MWBEs received just 5% of total city contract spend in FY25, or $2.44 billion of a $46 billion budget. He notes contract count rose to 65% but value share fell from 17% in FY24 to 8% in FY25.
chapters.title: Restler cites stagnant FY25 MWBE contracting numbers

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The Comptroller's Office releases a fantastic report each year on the City of New York's progress supporting MWBs that provides a detailed breakdown on where city agencies are doing well and where they're coming up short.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In FY25, MWBs received just 5% of the city's total contracting spend, 2.5%.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: $44 billion out of a $46 billion contract budget.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: These numbers have remained relatively stagnant for years.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Looking more specifically at contracts that are subject to MWBE goals under Local Law 174, there was an increase in the number of contracts going to MWBEs last year to 65%.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: 20,539 contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But the share of contract value going to MWBs fell from 17% back in FY24 to 8% in FY25, about half as much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: MWEs won more of the contracts in FY25, but got less of the money.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I commend the Office of MWBE for the increase in the number of contracts awarded to MWBEs, and I commend SBS for the increased number of certified MWBEs.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But I am concerned that MWBEs are only finding success in small-dollar contracts and not growing at the same pace, and spend on MWBEs is not growing at the same pace as our overall contract budget.

chapters.summary: Restler says average non-MWBE contracts were $3.6 million versus under $750,000 for MWBEs, and construction MWBEs received just over 10% of citywide contract value. He flags that Black-owned firms got 7% of MWBE contracts and Latino-owned firms 7.9%, with Black women and Latinas each around 1.2%.
chapters.title: Restler details disparities for Black, Latino, and women-owned MWBE firms

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The average contract registered to a non-certified firm, a non-MWBE, was $3.6 million.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But the average MWB contract was under $750,000, less than 25%.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is particularly notable in our construction contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: MWBEs received just over 10% of the citywide contract value.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There is also a deeply troubling, deeply troubling disparity within M.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: MWBE contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For all of the MWBE contracts awarded last year, black-owned firms account for just 7% of MWBE contracts, and Latino-owned firms account for 7.9%.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The city's black and Latino population are 22 and 29%, respectively, a majority of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The disparities are even worse when we account for gender.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Male-owned firms account for over eight times as many contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Male-owned MWBE firms account for over eight times as many contracts as female-owned firms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Firms owned by black women account for just 1.17% of MWBE contracts awarded.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And firms owned by Latinas account for 1.22%.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This data is just unacceptable, and I am keen to understand what efforts are underway in the new administration to open up more opportunities for black and Latino-owned businesses, especially businesses owned by black women and Latinas.

chapters.summary: Restler notes about 65% of FY25 MWBE contracts were registered retroactively, forcing small firms to front costs. He says nearly $33 billion in Local Law 174 contracts since FY22 have no subcontract records, with only about 9% of prime contracts reporting subcontract data.
chapters.title: Restler flags retroactive registration and missing subcontract data

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In FY25, about 65% of MWBE contracts were registered retroactively, meaning that the work began before the paperwork was done to be able to actually pay the company.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For a small firm, that means the company needs to front the funds to complete the work while they wait for the city to pay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That kind of risk can be untenable for a small business.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There are also significant gaps in the data that is reported to the public.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Since FY22, the city has registered nearly $33 billion in contracts

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: subject to Local Law 174 goals with no subcontract records whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just want to say that again.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: $33 billion in contracts subject to Local Law 174 MWB goals with no subcontract data whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Records exist for about 1,100 of the roughly 12,000 prime contracts, just about 9% of the total contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And more than 20 agencies, that's nearly half the city agencies, report nothing whatsoever on subcontracts during that time.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The Department of Design and Construction manages to report this data, so it can be done, but most agencies simply don't take the time or make the effort to report this information.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What this means is that there's potentially significant MWBE utilization happening every day with subcontractors that are owned by black, Latino, Asian, women-owned firms, but we have negligible data.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Without this data, there is no accountability.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And without accountability, there will be no improvement.

chapters.summary: Restler explains that human service contracts are exempt from MWBE goals but often use for-profit subcontractors that may be MWBEs. He introduces Intro 834 to require reporting on those subcontracts and calls for a pipeline for MWBEs to grow into larger prime contracts.
chapters.title: Restler discusses human services subcontracting and Intro 834

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This issue extends to our human service contracts as well.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Human service contracts are exempt from MWBE goals, but many of these contracts use for-profit subcontractors that may be MWBEs.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For example, consider a nonprofit shelter.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Operators...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: A nonprofit shelter operator hires a for-profit firm to deliver food or run security.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I've introduced legislation, Intro 834, which would require reporting on those subcontracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm hopeful that better reporting on subcontracts

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: will help us understand the MWBE landscape more broadly and identify more firms that we can support and connect to larger prime contracting opportunities that they may be qualified for.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I hope we hear more today about how the Mondani administration plans to increase MWBE contracting opportunities,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: especially through cultivating a pipeline of MWBEs, of successful MWBEs that are already contracting with the city so that they can grow and take on larger and larger contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm also keen to learn more about how we can elevate more black and Latino and especially black women and Latina firms to do more business with the city.

chapters.summary: Restler previews three additional bills: Intro 208 adding Middle Eastern and North African Americans to MWBE disparity studies, Intro 694 requiring targeted agency outreach when utilization goals are missed, and Intro 896 restricting non-compostable single-use cup contracts. He thanks staff and turns to Council Member Farías.
chapters.title: Restler introduces Intro 208, 694, and 896

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We'll also be hearing three pieces of additional legislation today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Intro 208, sponsored by Councilmember Shahana Hanif, would add Middle Eastern and North African Americans to the minority groups recognized under the city's MWBE program.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Firms owned by New Yorkers of Middle Eastern and North African descent are effectively invisible in our procurement data, and this bill would begin to change that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Intro 694, sponsored by Councilmember Farias, and thank you for joining us, would require agencies that miss their utilization goals to do something about it by conducting outreach and education targeted to the specific MWE categories where they fell short.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think this is a great bill.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And finally, Intro 896 got squeezed into this hearing, sponsored by Councilmember Epstein, and it would prohibit city agencies from entering into or renewing contracts to purchase non-compostable single-use cups with exceptions for health and safety emergencies and agreements already in place.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think this was an old Eric Botcher bill.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: No, not an old Eric Botcher bill, just kidding.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I want to recognize that the contract, and I want to thank again the staff who I thanked at the beginning for doing such a great job.

chapters.summary: Farías says agencies that repeatedly miss MWBE utilization goals must focus outreach on the specific categories where they fall short. She describes working with community-based organizations and ethnic media to reach businesses through trusted networks and require agency MWBE officers to monitor progress.
chapters.title: Council Member Farías speaks in support of Intro 694

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I would now like to turn it over to Councilmember Frias for an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Ressler, members of the Committee on Contracts, for holding today's hearing on MWBE utilization in city contracting and for allowing me a moment to speak in support of my bill, Intro 694.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: New York City has established utilization goals because we recognize that minority and women-owned businesses have historically been shut out of government contracting opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: But when an agency repeatedly fails to meet those goals, we cannot continue relying on the same broad outreach and expect a different result.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Intro 694 responds by requiring agencies to focus their outreach on the specific MWBE categories in which they are falling short.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: That means working with community-based organizations and the Office of Ethic and Community Media to reach businesses through trusted local networks and provide practical information about certification, procurement opportunities, and how to compete for agency contracts.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: This bill would also require agency MWBE officers to monitor progress within those categories and report on how these targeted efforts are being implemented.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: This creates a clear connection between the disparities an agency identifies, the corrective action it takes, and the results it produces.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We know there are qualified entrepreneurs across the city who are ready to do business with New York.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Too often, however, they are left to...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: trying to navigate an unnecessarily complicated procurement system without the relationships, information, or institutional access enjoyed by larger and more established firms.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The responsibility cannot remain entirely on small businesses to find their way into the room.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: When an agency consistently fails to reach a particular group of businesses,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The agency must be responsible for changing how it reaches them and continues to do so.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Intro 694 gives agencies a more focused way to close those gaps and gives the council a stronger basis for evaluating whether their improvement plans are producing actual results.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'd like to thank Chair Ressler again for hearing this piece of legislation, and thanks to my colleagues who have joined me as co-sponsors.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I really look forward to today's testimony from the administration, as well as hearing from the public and continuing the work together to move Intro 694 forward.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, folks, and thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.text: And if you have written copy of the testimony, please share them with the sergeants so that we can bring them up to the chair.

utterances.text: It's got to be something.
