chapters.summary: Michael J. Garner, the city's first Chief Business and Diversity Officer, introduces his background at the School Construction Authority and MTA. He appears with First Deputy Chief Business Diversity Officer Dwight Flynn, MOCS, and SBS colleagues to discuss the MWBE program.
chapters.title: Chief Business Diversity Officer Michael Garner introduces himself and his team

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Ressler and proposed bill sponsors, Fariz Hanif and Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: My name is Michael J.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Garner, and I serve as the city's first ever chief business and diversity officer.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: It is a pleasure to engage with you on all of our shared commitment to the advancement of the city's MWB program and to the health of the overall MWBE community.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: As someone who has served a significant portion of my career advancing MWBE programming, first at the New York City School Construction Authority for 15 years and at the MTA for 15 years, and now at the City of New York, I'm honored to be here.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Representing our program and City Hall along with my first deputy chief business diversity officer Dwight Flynn.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Also my colleagues at the Office of Contract Services, MOX, and the New York City Department of Small Business Services.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Considering our shared commitments towards continuous programmatic and policy improvement,

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: to the city's MWB program.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I am also here to share some of the great work that we have produced over the past three years, as well as to provide answers to the council's committee questions along with my MOX and SBS colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: As such,

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I would like to preface that my intent today is to respond to the contract of committee's questions and to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: However, we would be more than happy to schedule briefings with your respective offices to discuss matters raised today in need of other comments and information.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Since my time as the Chief Business Diversity Officer, we've achieved key MWBE successes and meaningful accomplishments that I would like to share with you today.

chapters.summary: Garner says FY26 first-half data show 33% MWBE inclusion for Local Law 1 agencies and 36% combined for city-funded agencies and authorities, with nearly $2 billion in awards. He cites FY25 as achieving the 30% aspirational goal for two straight years and over $6.9 billion in MWBE contracts citywide.
chapters.title: Garner reports FY26 MWBE inclusion and record contract awards

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: While we are working towards finalizing the past fiscal year's 26 full MWBE data, we remain confident that we are on track to continuing the positive

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: trajectory of our program been on these last handful of fiscal years.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: The following key metrics represent the city's performance in the first six months of the current administration, FY26, quarters three and four.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: 33% MWBE inclusion for agencies under Local Law 1.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Combined 36% MWBE inclusion for city-funded agencies and authorities.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Nearly $2 billion.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: in MWB contract awards.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: The overall outcomes of this administration in the first six months follow positive trends, further realizing our program's mission.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: In fact, last fiscal year, we achieved the city's aspirational 30% goal for agencies under Local Law 1, which was accomplished two straight fiscal years in a row.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We also set an MWBE record to over $2 billion in contracts awarded by agencies under Local Law 1 and one NYC

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: city record of $6.9 billion in MWBE contracts.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: These achievements are four straight years of MWBE contracts above $6 billion.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: That the city has awarded to city certified MWBEs under 1NYC.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: These contract awards is critical to support the city during our COVID era economic recovery by addressing the city's most important goods and services.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Needs while creating and promoting measurable economic activity in our local MWBE neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: In the city's last four fiscal years, city-certified MWBEs have secured just over $28 billion in contracts, a national record for any program of its kind.

chapters.summary: Garner says the MWBE small purchase method set records, totaling $350 million in FY25 and over $1 billion across three fiscal years. He lists state legislative wins and local policy changes, including raising the threshold to $1.5 million and securing B2G Now for reporting.
chapters.title: Garner highlights small purchase method and policy changes

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We also continue to prioritize MWBEs.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: by putting them in the program's critical path, leveraging the MWBE small purchase method, a procurement tool that allows for more streamlined processing contracting with city-certified MWBEs.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We set three straight fiscal records for use of this method, totaling $350 million

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: in MWB contracts using the method in FY25 alone and over $1 billion during the three fiscal years timeframe.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Lastly, we were able to secure New York State legislative victories and local policy program improvements that allowed us to enhance our available tools and better coordinate our efforts citywide.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: These include raise MWBE small purchase method threshold twice from $500,000 to $1.5 million.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Local Law 1 agency secured ability to self-register MWBE small purchase method contracts from the New York City Office of the Comptroller.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: EOs 26 and 34 better align MWBE program and provided agency guidance on creation of the creation of more equitable contracting opportunities wherever practical.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And to share and report MWBE's data to the CBDEO, funding was secured to evaluate and implement B2G Now as a tool to supplement the C.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: existing MWBE reporting capabilities.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: The system remains dependent on reliable data from authoritative source systems and does not replace Passport,

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: FMS, or the systems used by non-majorial entities, though will allow a more comprehensive near real-time citywide.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Performance reporting under one NYC program.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Establish weekly CompStat-like meetings to review key agencies'MWBE metrics, weekly discussions with agencies on barriers in preventing MWBE

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: in city contracting and discussing best practices solutions.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Currently coordinating with agencies on strategies to maximize the use of the MWBE small purchase method to its upper limits of $1.5 million.

chapters.summary: Garner says the administration supports the goals of Intro 208 and 694 and looks forward to further conversations. On Intro 834, he says Passport already captures required subcontract information, and on Intro 896, MOCS is still evaluating the bill.
chapters.title: Garner gives administration positions on Intro 208, 694, 834, and 896

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Regarding the bill scheduled to be introduced as part of this hearing,

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Intro Bill 208, we support the goal of evaluating emerging disparities in the city and look forward to further conversations with the bill sponsors.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Intro Bill 694, the Mayor's Office of Contract Services, MOX, supports the intention of this bill and look forward to having further conversations with the sponsor.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Intro Bill No.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: While we support the intent of this bill, based on MOC's review, Passport already captures the subcontract information required by the bill.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: including subcontractor's name, contract information, subcontract value, and the type of work.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Passport also supports HHS and lower-tier subcontractors, and MWBE certification information is sourced from SBS through FMS.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We look forward to further conversation with the sponsor.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Intro Bill 896.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: MOX is currently evaluating this bill, and we look forward to having further conversations with our partner agencies and the sponsor.

chapters.summary: Garner acknowledges more work remains and thanks City Hall leadership, MOCS Director Kim Yu, and SBS Commissioner Mania. He says the program supports MWBE businesses, local economies, and economic justice citywide.
chapters.title: Garner closes testimony with thanks and commitment to more work

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: In closing, we certainly recognize that there's more work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yet we remain appreciative of the opportunity to build on our progress, the leadership in City Hall, the dedication and competency of our oversight principals, Chief City

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Procurement Officer and MOX Director Kim Yu and SBS Commissioner Mania

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: are the collective commitment of our city and our city-affiliated agencies and authorities whose efforts have been the driving force behind the city's MWB achievements.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Lastly, and just as importantly, we recognize the Council's overall support of the MWBE program.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Our program is supportive of MWBE businesses and local economies and promotes economic justice citywide.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Restler acknowledges the Adams administration's MWBE contracting gains but asks why MWBE value share fell from 17% in FY24 to 8% in FY25. He asks Garner to evaluate overall performance and explain the significant decline.
chapters.title: Restler questions Garner on FY25 decline in MWBE prime contract value

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Councilmember Frias is going to let me know if she chooses to jump in at her discretion, because once I get going, I just get going.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chief Garner, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We really appreciate you being with us today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And, you know, I'll just say for a moment, I think that the Adams administration prioritized this issue and had a success in engaging in

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: contracting with more MWB firms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And there aren't many nice things I say about the Adams administration, so that's as close as I'll get to a compliment, and now move forward.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But I do want to recognize that sincerely.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know it's not easy.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just, I want to come back to some data to just kind of ground us because you were using some data in your presentation, in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I had some data points that I referenced in my opening.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, at a super high level, in FY25, the city had a contracting budget of about $46 billion, and MWBEs received $2.44 billion of that funds, about 5% of the total contract spend.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For the last few years, that percent has remained stagnant.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: MWB growth.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: has not kept pace with the growth of city contracting, which has increased.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Looking at just the 40% of contracts that are subject to Local Law 174 goals, or Local Law 1 as you reference it in your testimony, the value share of prime contracts going to MWEs declined significantly from

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: about 17% in FY24 to about 8% in FY25, about half as much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How do you evaluate this overall performance?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What was the cause of the significant decline from FY24 to FY25?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just at a high level, and then we can go into more specifics.

chapters.summary: Garner calls the Comptroller an ally but says the report excludes MWBE subcontractor activity and non-municipal agencies like SCA, NYCHA, Public Schools, EDC, and H+H. He says those five agencies hold 55-65% of city procurement spend and the city is focused on a OneNYC view.
chapters.title: Garner says Comptroller report omits subcontract and non-mayoral agency data

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So certainly we view city controller.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Office as an ally and a partner.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I've had a long-lasting positive relationship with City Controller Mark Levine.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I was on his transition team when he ascertained the office of the Manhattan Borough President.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We have a long working relationship.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We both agree that we're going to work in tandem.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: However, the city controller's report does not include any of the MWBE subcontractor activity

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: or totals, and it does not include any of the non-municipal agencies, including the School Construction Authority, NYCHA, the New York City Public Schools, EDC, and health and hospitals, where...

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Between 55 and 65 percent.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: of the city's procurement spend reside with those five agencies.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And so we are focused on a one NYC viewpoint of capturing all MWB activities, local law agencies, and the NUT.

chapters.summary: Restler agrees with the OneNYC orientation but says the Council and MOCS lack consistent data from non-mayoral agencies. He asks Garner to help get better data on those agencies and on subcontracting so the city can tell a different story.
chapters.title: Restler asks for better data from non-traditional agencies and subcontracting

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And to be clear, I think that's the right...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Orientation for you and your job.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The challenge we have, that MOX has, that all of us have, is we don't have access consistently to those non-mayoral agencies or the non-traditional agencies'data.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so the controller's got the data he has, and he's giving us analysis based on that data.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If you can help us, and MOX can help us, get better data on what those kind of non-traditional mayoral agencies are doing and what's happening on the subcontracting level, then we have a different story to potentially tell.

chapters.summary: Garner says the city is creating a new MWBE IT platform called B2G, modeled on New York State's system, to capture contract awards and payments centrally. He says the platform will go live within the fiscal year and will shift focus from awards to payments.
chapters.title: Garner describes B2G platform for real-time MWBE payments data

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So two things are happening, and I'm glad that you asked that question.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And so we have been working with creating a new MWBE information technology platform called B2G.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And it is the same platform that was instituted at the state of New York.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And my deputy here was in charge of instituting that program, that platform, at 97 different agencies and state authorities.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And what this new platform is going to do is it's going to not only allow us in a centralized manner to capture MWBE contract awards,

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: but more importantly, the payments.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And so we are now going to...

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: pivot from MWBE awards and highlighting the awards, but we're now going to more importantly focus on the payments of MWBEs.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We're currently working internally right now.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: That process will go live in a very, very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you expect the B2G to go live this year?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This fiscal year?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

chapters.summary: Restler asks whether B2G is a new platform and whether it will capture awards, spend, and subcontracting for every city agency. Garner confirms it will cover the Big Five agencies and provide one centralized platform for all MWBE activity.
chapters.title: Restler questions B2G scope and Big Five participation

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And just to make sure that I properly understand how it's worked at the state level.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So we're just so I get it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're expanding an existing state platform.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So that city agency or it's a new.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: No, it's a new platform that that that we issued an RFP and secure the services of a of a firm to help us build out this project.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Existing state resource.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Well, no.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So I was only using the state as an example of how the state.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So this is a new thing that we're creating.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so every city agency, so that data system or that platform will capture the awards and spend of every city agency's contracts?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And indicate whether they're MWEs and you think will comprehensively capture subcontracting as well through that system?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: DOE, NYCHA, health and hospitals, ED.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: DC and the school construction authority are all going to fully participate?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So what we agreed with the city controller, that we are going to create one centralized platform that will highlight all of our MWBE activity.

chapters.summary: Restler questions why the city is creating a new system when Passport already captures contract actions. He raises cost and operational concerns for procurement officials having to use an alternative system.
chapters.title: Restler asks why the city is not using Passport for MWBE data

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And can I just, this may not be a question for you, this may be a question for John, but...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Why not Passport?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We have an existing system that captures all of our contract actions.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just would assume that it's a cost and...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Operational challenge for every procurement official in the city of New York to have to now use an alternative system to capture this data, why not use our existing procurement system for gathering this information?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So I'll let John respond to that, but it's my understanding that the big five, as we call it, they do not.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Enter their information in a passport.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And so we wanted to create something that will, once again, have the opportunity for everyone to go to one centralized platform, look into the system, and observe all of the MWB activity, including

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: contract awards, but more importantly, the payments on those awards.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay, you want to jump in on why we didn't use Passport here as well?

chapters.summary: A MOCS representative says Passport's primary users operate under specific procurement governance, while the Big Five operate under different governance. Restler pushes back, noting the mayor got them to participate in B2G and asking why not Passport.
chapters.title: MOCS explains Passport governance and why Big Five do not use it

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Ressler.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And it's an honor and privilege to be here this morning.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is this your third time testifying this year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm not kidding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Keeping count, but I'm happy to see that you are.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're happy to see you, too.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: At least we haven't been so mean that you've chosen not to come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'll keep coming back as long as you're inviting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I believe just to take a step back for a moment about what the intent of Passport was to do, it's the city's...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sourcing and solutions portal for procurement activity, its primary users are agencies that are really operating under a very specific governance for procurement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The agencies that you were referencing operate under a different governance, and so I think that inherently creates a little bit of a challenge.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I totally appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think ultimately it's up to the mayor to tell them what to do.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If the mayor was able to get them these five, the big five, we'll call them that for the rest of the day to keep it simple.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If the mayor was able to get the big five or Chief Garner was able to get the big five to agree to do this with B2G to participate in B2G, why couldn't we get them to just participate in Passport?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think that's a question that might...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: naturally move into a deeper conversation that we're happy to participate in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: One thing I wanted to add, though.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The DOE just announced a series of procurement reforms, none of which make them subject to the PPB rules, none of which increase their transparency in a meaningful way, or provide the same level of oversight that you have of every other traditional mayoral agency.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just feel like it would have been simpler to use.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I know that Passport sucks and that everyone's frustrated with it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Or is that not how I'm supposed to describe it?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Passport, everyone's frustrated with Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I won't, it has its limitations.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But it just strikes me as challenging to create a whole new system that people are going to have to use to gather this information when we have an existing vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The one thing I will say about Passport, and I won't judge for or against.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You're not going to say on the record that it sucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I will simply state that that's the system that we're working with, and like anything, we work with what we have.

chapters.summary: Restler credits Council-funded Passport enhancements and asks for more detail on B2G implementation. He asks whether procurement officers and vendors must enter data themselves or whether B2G pulls automatically from existing systems.
chapters.title: Restler acknowledges Passport enhancements and asks about B2G timeline

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Totally.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Can I learn a little bit more about the people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There have been some enhancements, though, Council.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yes, there have, and I appreciate it, and we funded them from the Council side and pushed very hard for those resources and are excited to see them implemented.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So can I just ask a couple questions about B2G so I understand it?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So I'm going to defer to my top deputy who was responsible for implementing B2G at the state.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So can you, I guess, share any updates you can on the timeline for when you expect to see this implemented?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think if you could...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Give us some greater insight.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How is this data being implemented and gathered?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is it something that procurement officers and contractor and the vendors have to implement themselves?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Or is the data gathered from other systems already automatically?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah, just help shine some light for us.

chapters.summary: Dwight Flynn says B2G pulls source data from FMS, Passport, and SBS certification records, and aggregates prime and subcontractor MWBE activity. He says it will provide more real-time data so the city can manage opportunities and challenges rather than waiting for quarterly reports.
chapters.title: Dwight Flynn explains B2G data sourcing and real-time reporting

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: So let's really quick.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: First of all, thank you for having us here today, having me here today, chair and committee.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: To answer your question, the B2G system gets its source data from the owners of that data.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: So that would be, you know, FISA, FMS, or from passport marks, or SBS in terms of certification level data.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: And what it's really good at, what it's really good at, is essentially aggregating and reporting out on MWB activity at the prime and sub level.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: That's sort of its main function.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: And as such, and the other thing is, as we get that data on a more regular cadence, because as you know right now, we get quarterly reports from Passport, that type of thing, and an annual report.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: We'll get more real-time data.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: Because one of the frustrations we've been having, of course, is that you want to actively manage opportunities and challenges as they come up.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: If you're seeing them, you know, a month after the quarter is over, that's not always possible.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: And so B2G will allow the city's MWBE program to be managed on a more real-time basis to intercept challenges and take advantage of opportunities and, of course, disseminate best practices.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: The system itself, again, there's not a direct tie-in.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: It's not like it's electronically tied into Passport, but there are files that are shared on a regular cadence between MOCs and OTI B2G

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: such that the system is updated on a regular cadence, and agencies can go in and take a look at their MWBE contracts, make sure there are no errors, right?

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: And if there are errors, they go back to the original system and they fix it because that means there's an error somewhere in Pathward or FMS.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: And they can then run reports, the likes of which they can't run right now.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: They can project and they can plan around their MWB activity.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: Our goal always is to maximize MWBE.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: Availability and participation at every agency at every contract level.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: You need to have the tools to do that.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: And the city over the years has done an excellent job in pushing forward this

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: this policy.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: But, you know, as technology improves, we have to update with the technology.

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: And that's what BTG allows us to do.

chapters.summary: Restler notes only 9% of subcontracting information from traditional mayoral agencies is reported in Passport, with DDC a rare good performer. He asks how B2G will help if agencies are not entering subcontract data into Passport or FMS.
chapters.title: Restler questions whether B2G will solve missing subcontract data

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just forgive my ignorance here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But just help me to understand it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If it's from Passport, we're not getting that information in Passport now.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, the controller's report and what we reviewed found that we're seeing 9% of subcontracting information from the traditional mayoral agencies is reported in Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: DDC seems to do a good job, and everybody else seems to be pooping the bed.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're not taking this seriously at all.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so 90% of our contracts are not getting– the subcontracting information is not getting reported to Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We have no information.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We can't do a global– we can't give a global answer on how much money is going to MWBEs because we don't know what's happening on the subcontracting side.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I feel like there's actually a good story, good news story for the city to be telling.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's part of the reason I introduced my legislation around the human services, right?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I won't go down that rabbit hole, but we don't have the data.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So Passport, I feel like if the information is feeding from Passport into this, it's not going to help us.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If it's feeding from FMS.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So we know the payments, but a payment's going to the prime, right?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The payment doesn't go directly to the sub.

chapters.summary: Garner says City Hall has emailed all agency commissioners to ensure third-party contractors enter MWBE payment data into Passport timely. He says MOCS will generate a report he expects to see Friday.
chapters.title: Garner says City Hall is pressing commissioners on Passport reporting

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So let me just, we, in a more proactive measure, from a city hall perspective, we have sent

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: emails to all of the agency commissioners, asking them to ensure that their third-party contractors and consultants are entering their MWBE payment data into Passport on a timely basis.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We are monitoring that now.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are you seeing any improvement?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We just started this this year.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We are now going to run a report with MOX.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I will see that report on Friday.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: But we are targeting...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Mark tells me that running these reports through Passport makes people's head explode and that it takes a long time and that it's very painful and it's challenging to get right.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: John has assured me that his staff is going to work with my staff in order to generate the report.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So we're expecting a report this Friday.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

chapters.summary: Restler says even a jump from 9% to 50% would still leave half of subcontract data missing, and notes 20 agencies reported zero subcontracting information for four years. Garner says the city is going directly to agency commissioners to enforce contract requirements.
chapters.title: Restler asks how data will improve if agencies are not reporting

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So we're going to set up a briefing soon to go through it, to hope that we're starting to actually see the data information.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Look, I welcome that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I guess.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm hopeful that that will work.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But just help me then.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Let's just say, for argument's sake, it doesn't, that we continue, or maybe say it works really well, and you go from 9% to 50%, which would be remarkable and a huge accomplishment, but we're still not getting the subcontracting data for half the contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How are we actually going to get the data if these agencies are not reporting to FMS?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There were 20 agencies that reported zero information on their subcontracting over the last four years.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Didn't take this seriously at all.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We are going directly to the agency commissioners.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We have confidence and faith that those agency commissioners are going to require their staff to work with and enforce.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: the contract requirements, which calls for MWBE or subcontracting payments to be entered into Passport on a regular basis.

chapters.summary: Restler says reporting subcontract data is already law and management from City Hall plus public accountability are both critical. Garner agrees to work with the Council to make public which agencies are sharing subcontracting data and which are not.
chapters.title: Restler pushes for public accountability on agency subcontract reporting

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really appreciate you saying that because, look, this is a management issue.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is the law.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This has already been the law that they have to report this information.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think we passed another bill that the Speaker passed earlier this year that further underscored this is the law, that this has to be reported, and agencies don't do it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think DDC does it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Because for a variety of reasons, but I think they have a good new story to tell because they do a terrible job on their, they don't do a great job on their primes, and so they need to highlight their subs or it would be really ugly, so they try to share the information.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I don't know why other agencies don't do it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you have insight into why other agencies don't take this seriously?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I've asked the question, and once again, we proactively now are reaching directly out to agency commissioners on a regular cadence.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And I'm confident that agency commissioners will enforce their respective contract requirements.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really appreciate you saying that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really believe strongly that public accountability is key to actually getting agencies to change behavior.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Management from City Hall and public accountability are both critical.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Can we work together to ensure that this information is made public on a regular basis of what agencies are actually sharing the subcontracting data and what aren't so that we know who's taking subcontracting?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: To MWB seriously and who isn't?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Certainly.

chapters.summary: Restler says without subcontract data the city cannot celebrate large sums flowing to Black, Latino, Asian, and women-owned firms. He asks what added value B2G provides if the information is coming from Passport, and Garner cites the Big Five and one centralized portal.
chapters.title: Restler asks what B2G adds if Passport already feeds it

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We, once again, we view the city council as a partner.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: A win for us is a win for you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Well, I just, generally, I don't mean to beat a dead horse here, but like,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: inevitably, we're doing a lot of subcontracting to MWBEs, but without the data, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we don't, there's, I presume, very large sums of money that are flowing out the door to black, Latino, Asian, and women-owned firms every single day, but we don't have any information to actually celebrate that or not, and the information we're getting is so...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: sclerotic, it's inconsistent, that we can't tell a story.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I think the way the Comptroller's Office over years now has handled their report by saying, we don't look at the subcontracting data because it's just too uneven and inconsistent and it's too fractured a story,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: is really important.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I appreciate that you're making this a priority and that you're trying to fix it and you're bringing a management orientation toward telling the agencies they have to take this seriously.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're very excited to see that information showing up in Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So then just not to belabor my initial point, but if they are going to be putting that information to Passport, that's how it's getting into B2G.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What's the added value that B2G has if we're just getting that information in Passport?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: The added value is once again– For the big five.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: The big five and also having one centralized portal.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: or information system where you can look at all of the MWBE activity and metrics for the city.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And is there any other planned uses of B2G beyond the kind of data and accountability?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: It's a tool which allows agencies to better enforce their MWB requirements based upon payments.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about Garner's contract-stat approach and how often B2G will receive uploads from FMS and Passport. Garner says reporting will be near real-time and transformational because the city has historically measured success by awards rather than payments.
chapters.title: Restler asks about CompStat-like meetings and data cadence

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I know I really appreciated your testimony where you highlighted that you're kind of taking a contract stat-like approach of...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Engaging a contract stat or, you know, comp stat-like approach.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm the contracts chair.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think about things in the contracts that way.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's not how the world looks.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I should pause and just say we're joined by Councilmember Althea Stevens, who I lovingly refer to as the vice chair of this committee because–

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: She refuses the title, but I give it to her anyway because she is so passionate about contracting reform and making sure especially our nonprofit partners get paid, and I really appreciate her expertise.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you for being here, Councilmember Stevens, and jump in with questions whenever you'd like.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we have Councilmember Vernikoff on Zoom, Brooklyn's own.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us, Councilmember Vernikoff.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is this data, the data will be valuable to you based on how often you're getting uploads from FMS and Passport feeding in.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So are you expecting weekly reports, monthly reports?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How do you anticipate utilizing the data in this new system?

chapters.summary: Garner explains that a $10 million contract awarded five years ago may only be 50% actualized, so payments better measure success. Restler notes payments are often less than awards and asks how this affects vendors working at risk.
chapters.title: Garner says payments are a better barometer than contract awards

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: The cadence of the reporting is as to white flint and kid almost in real time.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And this is going to be transformational because the city has historically evaluated their MWBE successes based upon contract awards.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: The more important metric here is payments.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But payments are less than awards, right, often?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Well, once contract matures, the payments will, at some given point in time, they will catch up.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Hopefully.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And so, for example, the estate has utilized this system for decades.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: They capture awards, but they capture, more importantly, the payments on those awards.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So, for example.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: If we report a $10 million contract that was awarded five years ago, not to exceed $10 million,

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: at the duration of that contract, after five years, if only...

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: 50% of that contract has been actualized, you've overstated the success.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So converting from contract awards now to payments is a better barometer of success.

chapters.summary: Restler notes 65% of MWBE contracts leave vendors working before registration and 35% are not registered for more than a month after the start date. He says the city must pay smaller MWBE firms on time if they are to grow into larger contracts.
chapters.title: Restler questions retroactive registration and delayed payment to MWBEs

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I guess it should probably get me to start asking you questions about how 65% of...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: MWB contracts leave vendors working at risk and doing work before contracts are registered and they're actually getting paid.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So it will also show that we're not doing a very good job of actually paying these firms that are often smaller firms that can't afford to wait for months or years to get paid

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: and that too many of our agencies don't have their act together and are delaying payment.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So it may also tell a story that's not all that pretty for the city.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Well, it's my understanding that this administration is taking that very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Is also my understanding that there has been a procurement reform committee that has been established to look at the time that it's taken to award contracts and the time that it's taken to pay

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: vendors and contractors.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I welcome the Mumdani administration's kind of earnest focus on how to make government work better.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know that the intentions are there.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This stuff is hard.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Administration after administration has struggled with these issues.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: These are evergreen challenges that, frankly, have not improved sufficiently over a long period.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: period of time, despite many mayors saying this is a priority and that they're going to fix it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I just want to highlight 35% of MWB contracts have not been registered for more than a month after the start date.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So when we're looking more closely at when people are actually getting paid, we're going to see that we're not doing a very good job of paying these folks.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And, and

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If we want these smaller MWB firms that are receiving smaller city contracts to continue to grow and to get larger and larger contracts in the city, which I know is our shared priority here, we need to pay them.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we can't put them in untenable situations where they're waiting for months or years to get paid for the work that they've already done.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think I'll complain to other people on another day about our failure to pay people on time.

chapters.summary: A MOCS representative says Passport Release 6 introduced a centralized workflow for recording subcontractor utilization and payments. Restler asks whether the city now has a better understanding of the subcontractor landscape, and MOCS says the tools exist but data coverage still needs follow-up.
chapters.title: MOCS cites Passport Release 6 subcontracting improvements

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Chair Ressler, if I may just add to this point before we move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If you were to move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The controller's report was a look back on the performance of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But since then, particularly with MOX and Passport, we did have Release 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And Release 6 did introduce a new centralized workflow that included a better way of recording and reporting subcontractor utilization, payments to subcontractors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Tracking the performance of the subcontractor utilization goals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so that data does exist today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So you're seeing a significant increase in...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that information will be available for city agencies to consume.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that the report that Chief Gardner referenced that is coming to him on Friday?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I believe Chief Garner is talking about the subcontractor payments that are recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, yes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So you think now, based on your expertise and the improvements in Release 6, that we actually have a much better understanding of the subcontractor landscape today than we did a year ago?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I would say it's fair to say that we have the tools now and the data available that will allow us to address the issue, which we agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's a management, it's an oversight, management performance issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we just want to be able to what

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: MOX is always trying to do, get better data and make that more available so that we can review and make more informed decisions.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But you don't yet have an understanding of, let's say, what percent of the subcontracts citywide are actually captured here so that we know how many of them are MWBs.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think that's something that we would be able to provide, but we'd have to follow up.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think we'd love to follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll just take a step back to say I'm grateful that this is a priority that you all have identified and that you're working on and that the new administration is really digging in on how do we do a better job of gathering this data comprehensively of subcontracts happening and how many are going to MWBs, and you're including the big five.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think those are all the right things to be doing, and I really want to commend you for it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know better than me whether creating a new technology platform was necessary to do this or not, but we're down that course, and I hope that it's successful.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I continue to be skeptical that we're going to get the information into Passport that we need, but it sounds like everybody's trying, and that you're trying from a management perspective, you're trying from a platform improvement perspective, and we'll all push together.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm very happy to be a loud and obnoxious council member saying to agencies, do your damn job and report this data.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's really important.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So let me know how I can be that partner as well.

chapters.summary: Restler asks again why MWBE prime contract value fell from 17% in FY24 to just over 8% in FY25. Garner says he needs to follow up but cites efforts to maximize prime opportunities, including a $400 million contract to Hispanic-owned Intercom Security Systems.
chapters.title: Restler returns to FY24-FY25 decline in prime contract value

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I did just, before we went down this rabbit hole, which I really did enjoy and found insightful, I just want to come back to the initial question I was asking you, Chief, which is, in FY20,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: According to the local law 174 metrics, about 17% of contract value went to MWBEs.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And then in FY25, we were at half that number, just over 8%.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you help us understand why did we see that significant decline year over year?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I would need to follow up.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And once again, I believe that we are now better equipped to capture the prime and the sub.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I can tell you and give you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm just referring to primes.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yes, because I don't have the sub data.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that we've been working internally in order to maximize prime contract opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: For example, we worked with SBS and with DCAS on a arm-on-arm security guard contract.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: That was the first time that that contract had been issued, the RFP.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We were zealous of breaking down the contract, disaggregating it, as opposed to having one larger contract.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We now have four.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We had a series of meetings and invited MWBE firms to DCAS.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I'm proud to announce that we've awarded a $400 million contract to an Hispanic-owned firm, almost one of the largest contracts in the history ever awarded to Hispanic-owned firms.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: The name of the firm is Intercom Security Systems.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: They have a major prime contract.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So we're focusing on...

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: on creating opportunities for our MWBEs at the prime level.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's helpful.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We would like to get some clarity on what happened from 24 to 25 and why we saw that reduction.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So if that's not something you're prepared to speak to today, we would definitely appreciate a follow-up there.

chapters.summary: Restler notes the average MWBE contract was about $750,000 versus $3.65 million for white male-owned firms. Garner attributes the disparity to lack of access to capital, surety bonding, and right-sized contracting, and says the city is working to create prime opportunities.
chapters.title: Restler asks about average MWBE contract size disparity

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I just want to kind of continue to harp on the issue of the value of MWBE contracts relative to non-MWBE contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So the data we looked at from FY25 was that the average MWBE contract was about $750,000.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The average non-MW white male-owned firm, I should just say it that way, right?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The average contract for a white male-owned firm was $3.65 million.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you explain what you think accounts for this disparity?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, that's more than four times differential, average of a white male-owned firm versus a non-white male-owned firm.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Why do you think we have such an extreme disparity there?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So, I mean, it is not unique to only the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I can tell you at the state.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: 75% of MWB contract awards are awarded at the sub-level as opposed to the prime level.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: When you factor in the lack of access to capital, when you factor in the lack of access to surety bonding, when you factor the lack of the right size contracting for MWBE firms, you will always see that.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: But we are working internally, certainly with...

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: with our partners at SBS, access to capital programs, the bundling of contracts at the agencies, designing smaller packages,

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: and having the ability to go out and recruit MWBEs and put them in the contracting critical path that they can bid as primes.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Because when in a contract as a prime, as you know, you are in control of your own destiny.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And so we are very focused on creating opportunities for our MWBE firms at the prime level.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Working as a subcontractor, hey, listen, it's a good business for some, but let's not fool ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We need to do a more effective job of creating prime opportunities for our MWBE firms.

chapters.summary: Restler says the city has done well connecting MWBEs to small contracts through the $1.5 million procurement cap. Garner and MOCS clarify that agencies can solicit MWBE pricing but still must consider best value and cannot simply award to any vendor.
chapters.title: Restler and MOCS discuss small purchase method and competition

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And to be clear, the disparity I'm referencing is between prime contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But I do want to kind of harp on that point, which is we have–

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: we've clearly done a very, I think, an admirable job as a city of connecting more MWBEs to small contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Through the $1.5 million procurement cap without a competitive process and being able to select an MWBE for work.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Well, let me, we, one of the first things that we did when we came to the administration that we changed the name of the non-competitive.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: It is not non-competitive.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Agencies have the ability to go out in the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Solicit prices only from MWBE firms as long as that pricing is a line.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: With historical pricing, the agency has the ability to award the contract.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Bless you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: The agency has the ability to award the contract right there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: But, and so we've...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It can go through a competitive process to try to get the best price, but they also don't need to go through a competitive process if that's just the fastest procurement vehicle and they want to move quickly.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: John, do you want to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There's still an obligation to have some level of consideration for price and what operates is the best value to the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I hear what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Well, I don't want there to be a misunderstanding that there is a straight line to a particular vendor that's an MWB that excludes any other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We want to give due consideration to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But the important part is that there's a dedicated space right now for those MWBs to operate and have that ability to get those awards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so I think that's more the...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Maybe I'll say it a different way.

chapters.summary: Restler says MWBEs win 65% of contracts but only 8% of spend, with average awards of $750,000. He asks how the city will help MWBEs already performing well grow into larger contracts rather than remaining a fast small-purchase route.
chapters.title: Restler pushes for a pipeline from small contracts to larger prime work

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Agencies can more quickly– oh, you guys are ready for questions.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, I get carried away.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll just finish this, and then I'll pass it to you guys.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Agencies have a faster procurement vehicle to go to MWBEs for under $1.5 million than not.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So there's an incentive there.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If you want to get something out the door quickly and get the work done to engage in MWBE for the local law 174, five priority areas.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're connecting, you know, city traditional, the non-Big Five city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's like 65% of contracts are going to MWBs.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That's a positive thing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But it's for a teeny fraction of the total spend.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And what I'm...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's, I think, the same point you're making about subs.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Also, for these small contracts where you're the prime, which is most of what MWEs are getting, they're getting very small contracts under $1.5 million.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Their average spend is $750,000, which is not nothing, but it's not when the average city contract is four times that amount.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There's a real question.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How do we build that pipeline?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How do we help engage the MWBEs that have city contracts, that are working with the city, that are demonstrating that they're effective, that they're doing a good job?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: How do we help them grow to take on larger contracts so that they're not just seen as a faster route to procurement for under $1.5 million?

chapters.summary: Garner says the city is starting to see change, pointing to a $400 million MWBE award. SBS Chief of Staff Haris Khan highlights the Contract Financing Loan Fund, one-on-one technical assistance, and the NYC Contracting Summit with over 100 agencies and resources.
chapters.title: SBS describes capital, technical assistance, and contracting summit programs

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I will answer that, and I want to defer and turn it over to SVS to talk about some of the supporting programming that they have for MWBEs.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: But I will tell you, we are starting to see a change.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I mean, the mere fact that we have the ability to award a $400 million contract to an MWB,

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: MWBE tells us that what we're putting in place is working.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And so your question is that we have to have the ability to equip our MWBE firms with access to capital, surety bonding assistance,

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner

utterances.text: So get upfront capital at a roughly 3% interest rate, much lower than market rate, and start delivering on the work that they have been engaged with a contracting agency.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And that's just one of the variety of services.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We have one-on-one technical assistance, capital access support, some legal help available, educational programming.

utterances.text: Not to be so blunt, but I think access to capital is really important, and I'm glad that you both mentioned that and you're focused on it and trying to help in that regard.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But I actually think as a city, we need a much more proactive approach where we're identifying MWB vendors that are doing a really excellent job with smaller contracts

utterances.text: Let's help them.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I just feel like we need a proactive, deliberate strategy to engaging those vendors.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That doesn't– that's not a pretty picture, right?

chapters.summary: Stevens asks how often the office reviews agency performance and what happens when agencies consistently miss goals. Garner says the city holds weekly MWBE CompStat meetings, generates monthly data from the Big Five, and brings issues to agency commissioners.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What accountability and compliance mechanism has been put in place since you've taken this often?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How often does your office review agency performances?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And what happens when an agency consistently misses its goals?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We call them the MWBE CompStat meetings.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And we want to look at their metrics, and we're generating data now once a month from the big five.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Slimmer to none than anything when they have to do this annually and the likeliness of them getting in.

chapters.summary: Farías says the city is not using the data in front of it or ensuring utilization goals and improvement plans reach underserved communities. She calls for bigger thinking to ensure Black women, Latinas, and other women of color actually get contracts.
chapters.title: Farías calls for using data, utilization goals, and improvement plans more aggressively

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I think that's part of the reason why we're looking at legislation.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: It's part of the reason why we're having this hearing and we've had this hearing year after year in the council.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Realistically, we are not utilizing the data in front of us.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We're not seeing utilization goals.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Coming up with plans or even doing the outreach necessary in communities where we're lacking certification, where we know businesses exist

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: and we're not getting them in to take 20 lists and make sure 15 out of those 20 people that we're going to promote to an organization or an agency

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: for a $7.5 million contract is either a woman and or a black woman and or a Latina.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: etc.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Like, I think that is what we're really talking about here and what we're trying to get to at the crux of.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I know you folks know this as well, but I think we need to put bigger thinking hats on when we're looking at these, the data's in front of us along with the utilization goals and potentially these improvement plans on how to get more people in.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: To ensure that they're actually

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: getting the contracts that are afforded to them by the taxes they pay and being a part of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I look forward to getting the response on the question that I asked before.

chapters.summary: Khan says 33% of the certified MWBE pool is African-American businesses, which Farías contrasts with one in 1,000 contracts for Black women. Garner says he is taking the issue personally and promises to broaden contract awards to all certified groups.
chapters.title: Khan says 33% of certified MWBEs are African-American; Garner says it is personal

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And I'd love to hear from you folks.

utterances.text: Shark, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I do have the, so it's 33% of the certified pool is African-American certified businesses.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a pretty big percentage comparatively to looking at hearing the number of one out of 1,000 for black women getting a contract in New York City.

utterances.text: I can assure you that we are having internal conversations.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I'm taking this personal.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yeah, it's personal to me too.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: That we have to do a better job, and we will do a better job.

utterances.text: It's not where we want it to be, but it's gradually improving because we have an emphasis on it.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
