chapters.summary: Farías says entrepreneurs find the certification and contracting process convoluted, paperwork-heavy, and time-consuming. She asks whether subcontractors will be included in utilization goals and improvement plans if the bills pass, and MOCS says the administration will incorporate new legal requirements.
chapters.title: Farías urges streamlining and asks if subcontractors will be in improvement plans

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: You know, I think also, at least from my first term and coming into the second term, we constantly hear from people, from entrepreneurs and small businesses, that this process is convoluted.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Paperwork is intense.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: It's time-consuming.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: There's streamlining that has to happen.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: There's simplification that has to happen in order for, like, our folks and our communities to actually compete.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Like there's a level of competition that we have to also help folks stream.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: line to improve these numbers.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And even in the subcontracting process, making sure payments go out first to those people despite the completion of the job.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Like there's a lot of steps that we as a city have to rectify that we've been talking about for a lot of years that I hope we can get to really soon.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Just in my last thought, I'd love to hear

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: you know, if and when these bills pass on the subcontracting side for a council member, for chair wrestler's bill, excuse me, will they then be included in this level of reporting for,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: in connection to my bill for the utilization goals and the improvement plans?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Will they be a part of, the subcontractors be a part of those plans?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, folks, so much for the time.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Restler asks for the percentage of certified MWBEs that are Black, Latino, Asian, and white women. Khan says African-American firms are 33%, Asian 23%, Hispanic 19%, white women 26%, and women overall are 55% of the program.
chapters.title: Restler asks Khan for breakdown of certified MWBE demographics

utterances.text: Thank you both for, I think, totally spot on questions that I really strongly, strongly agree with the line of questioning and the points that you were both making.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you for making them so persuasively.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just want to come back to what Councilmember Frias was asking about Mr.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Khan.

utterances.text: Just want to make sure that I understand it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So you're telling us that from

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: the total number of certified MWBEs, could you just break down what percentage is black, what percentage is Latino, what percentage is Asian, what percentage is white women?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I guess it's just the data I'm looking at is different, so that's why I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So it fluctuates year to year.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There's recertifications, there's certifications.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The controller might be looking at FY25.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I did want to note that...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Can you give me the number on Latinos?

chapters.summary: Restler notes Black firms are 33% of certified MWBEs but receive less than 7% of MWBE contracts, while Latino firms are 19% of certifications but less than 8% of contracts. He says the city is not achieving the program's goals if these firms are not contracting at scale.
chapters.title: Restler contrasts certification rates with contract award disparities

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I just want to make sure that I'm thinking about things the right way.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Please feel free to correct me if I am.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We'll start with black firms as an example.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: About 33% of registered MWB, so we're doing a good job on outreach and reaching black firms across the city, helping to get them registered, certified.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But less than 7% of MWB contracts are going to black-owned firms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that approximately, do I have the right contrast?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I defer to the City Hall colleagues here on the, if we're looking at Local Law 1 or 1NYC, but what we have, the certification numbers is what you're citing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the controller's report.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is what he had in his report for Local Law 174.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I just want to highlight, 33% of certified MWEs, black, just less than 7% of contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For traditional city agencies going to black owned firms, 19% of contracts of vendors that are certified or Latino owned, and less than 8% of contracts are going to Latinos,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: just as examples.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So those are areas where we just clearly have a lot more work to do.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I appreciate your point, Chief Garner, that

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, there's been an effort to improve things, but the status where we are today is profoundly unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I just think this has to be a major priority for this administration to start engaging black and Latino firms in particular in a real way because they're not.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We are not achieving the goals of our MWB programs if we're not engaging those firms and contracting with those firms at scale.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that my colleagues have asked the questions around what efforts are being made to boost participation, especially of women of color-led businesses, and I just really want to underscore I hope that that is happening on steroids.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll do a handful.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Well, let me not overpromise.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll keep going until Vice Chair Stevens tells me she wants to jump back in.

chapters.summary: Restler notes significant variation in MWBE performance across agencies, with DDC performing better than the Health Department. He asks what intervention the city uses when an agency is not taking MWBE contracting seriously, and Garner describes meetings with commissioners and ACCOs.
chapters.title: Restler asks how the city intervenes with underperforming agencies like Health

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There is significant variation in MWB performance across city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Some do pretty well.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Some seem to not care about this at all.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In the previous administration, just looking at the data from previous years, I imagine this administration, everybody will make it a big priority and everything will be perfect.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But, for example, DDC seemed to be performing significantly better than the health department, for example.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you just walk me through an agency like the health department failing to do its job, not taking contracting with MWE seriously, not making it a priority?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What's your intervention to try to get them to course correct?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So once again, we're looking at data on a more regular basis.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: I'm having meetings with agencies and at the committee.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: missioner level, working with their ACCOs and working with their MWB staff, giving them the support that they need, creating programming that would allow them to do a more effective job in their contracting.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: So we are up close and personal.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And, you know, it has to be the...

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Error of transparency and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And we are using the data in order to drive effective change at these agencies, allowing them to do a more effective job of broadening their contract awards.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For the public, what's the best real-time information or kind of regularly updated information that we can access to understand how agencies are performing throughout the fiscal year?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Well, certainly with the introduction of B2G, it's going to give us like almost real-time of contract award data.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And also, more importantly, once again, the payment data.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And so once the system is fully operational, we can generate data almost on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I think we'll have to figure out a...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Public reporting cadence of the B2G data as that platform comes online.

chapters.summary: Restler says smaller agencies often perform better than larger ones, and SBS was among the worst performers in the latest Comptroller report with zero subs. Khan says SBS is a very small contracting agency and will follow up on the data discrepancy.
chapters.title: Restler questions SBS's own MWBE contracting performance

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I guess I don't mean to pick on anybody.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is the previous administration, I guess, that I can still pick on because it's the data we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we found that generally some of the smaller agencies have had greater success in both their percentage of contracts that go to MWBs and...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The percentage of their overall contract budget that goes to MWBEs, and that larger agencies have not been able to kind of integrate MWB prioritization as effectively.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know that's an oversimplified analysis, but...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, for example, Chief Khan, in the latest...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Controller report, SBS was among the worst performers in your own contracting with MWBEs and recorded zero subs, which may be the types of contracts that you all have.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You may not have as many subcontracts, but just how are you as an agency, just as an example, trying to course correct and do better in this new administration?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we are very, very small contracting.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We're an incredibly small contracting agency, but we can get back to you on what we've done on MWB.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We usually have performed at the highest of the pack most of the years in our MWB performance.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So whatever the data discrepancy is here, we'll look at it and we'll follow up.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, I would imagine this is...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, a real priority for you all, considering you've got a deputy commissioner that's responsible for this portfolio of certifying firms and doing outreach and engagement.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know that most of the folks you contract with are nonprofits, you know, bids, et cetera, but local development corporations.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yes, we just don't have capital dollars.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We don't do construction in the city.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We don't run incredibly complicated programs.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We do direct service work.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Most of it is done in-house.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Some of it is done through contracted partners.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: No, but you're the agency sitting at the table.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: These guys don't, none of the people to your left do any contracting.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So you're the person I can pick on.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it's just to say as an example, you're...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: SBS, which is like your mission, is...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: this work still in the relatively small amount of contracting you're doing, at least for FY25 and the controller's most recent report, because that's the data that I use as my Bible, wasn't contracting with MWDs at the scale that we should be.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I can go through the specifics if it's helpful, but I think we just want to...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Underscore that every agency needs to make this a priority.

chapters.summary: Restler explains Intro 834 would require nonprofits with large city contracts to report whether their for-profit subcontractors are MWBEs. MOCS says Passport already records subcontractor and payment information, and Restler says he will pull the bill only if updated data shows compliance.
chapters.title: Restler asks whether administration supports Intro 834 on nonprofit subcontracting

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think we've gone pretty deep into subcontracting, but I don't think I've asked specifically about my bill.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So let me just do that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: As I think I've explained, we have some large nonprofit contracts, like with a shelter operator or a close-to-home operator or something like that, where there are significant subcontracts to for-profit firms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In fact, in the DHS space, it's been where we've seen a lot of corruption over the years, unfortunately, so we need to have transparency and accountability there.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is our legislation that would require nonprofits to report on whether their subs are MWBEs something that the administration supports?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think it's consistent with the broader mission that you're laying out around better data around subcontracting so we can tell a more comprehensive story of how we're contracting with MWBEs.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Let me defer to Mark first, and then I will hone in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Chair Ressler.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's something that we're looking at, but just given what I was sharing at the hearing today

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: about the information that we're collecting, the ability to report on level of subcontracting across all contracts, not just

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: MWBEs, but any prime contractor that has a subcontractor, it's being recorded and reported in Passport along with payment information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that's something that I think when you look at what currently exists today and you compare it against what this bill is recommending, it may seem like there might be some duplicative work here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm, if, but we're certainly happy to have a.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In fact, the improvements from release six are, have been so dramatic and there has been like a sea change of compliance with subcontracting reporting and passport in the intervening year since the last controller's data and report, then.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm happy to pull back my legislation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But I don't believe that that is the case, and I think that we need this data, and I think we need this data across the board.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I am eager to see updated data from you all on how we're doing on the subcontracting piece, but I think this is going to be very hard to actually get agencies to comply and submit this data.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So, and it sounds to me like B2G is kind of dependent on agencies actually.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Taking this on seriously and submitting their subcontracting information into Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I appreciate that we have City Hall support on this, but like...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This has been impressively not done across the board.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Like agencies have clearly not cared, despite this being local law and despite this being a priority.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So if you can show me a data report that shows you have all this information, I will tell the speaker that I no longer want to pass this bill.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I don't believe such a data report exists, but I'm open to being persuaded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Councilmember Chair Ressler, I'm sure that Director Yu would be more than happy to incorporate this into the regular cadence that she has with your office to discuss

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: viewing this data on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just, to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: In the last controller's report, 9% of subcontracts were reporting to Passport.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So unless you've got a report that shows me that 100% is happening now, we're going to push this legislation and we're going to be really aggressive in trying to support your efforts because this is what Chief Garner is saying is a major priority for him.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You correct me if I'm saying anything incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There's a major priority that we get all agencies to report their subcontracting data so we can see where funds are going to MWBEs.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I, you know, so, but if Director Yu and you have a report that can show me that we're magically doing this today and we're doing 9% a year ago, I will be thrilled.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I might not have had the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I would have had the hearing for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But I wouldn't have spent half the time talking about this topic that I think is so important.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I will just say again for the record, for Councilmember Brewer's benefit, that I think it's over the last four years there was $33 billion in spending that's subject to Local Law 174.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: where there's no subcontracting data reported into Passport whatsoever in aggregate over that four-year period.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That is a lot of money where we have no idea whether we're supporting MWEs with it or not.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it makes Chief Garner look bad, right?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Because he could be getting credit for billions of dollars that are going to MWBs.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We might be supporting more black women-owned firms and more Latina firms and more other firms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Through subs that we don't have the data for.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So if that data is there now and we're doing a better job and we're making the city all priority, I will be the happiest man in the city council.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But I am waiting to be persuaded.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I think I've asked enough about my bill.

chapters.title: Brewer asks about certification complexity and state streamlining

utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer, before I keep going, do you want to jump in?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One question that I hear all the time, and again, this is on the larger scale, is it's too complicated to apply.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is that not true, to be an MBWB?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I hear that all the time.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Council Member Burr, thank you so much for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I was next door.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I wasn't far, just so it's clear.

utterances.text: process faster for a New York City firm that wants to apply to city and state certification.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Because essentially, if you're interested in city contracting, you probably could also be very interested in state contracting and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So they would be the same when you say streamlined?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Not necessarily the same, but we are working very closely with the state portal, and they do have some functionality where an applicant that is applying through the state's portal could select themselves as a person interested in the city portal.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What's the timing on that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have any sense?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They've just launched the state-facing portion of it, and we're in active conversations.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's somewhat of a tech project, so it will require deep coordination, but we're really excited on the prospects of that.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And as of right now, separate from that potential even further streamlining effort that we are underway, if

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: a MWBE firm approaches the city and is a state-certified firm, we're looking at an average of, and we aim to deliver a response to them, a certification decision to them within a month if they have that state certification.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Again, it really depends on ownership structures.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: If you tell us you have 15 partners in your business, that will complicate things because now you've got 15 different sets of ownership documents we have to review.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what percentage of certified MWBEs win city contracts, saying business owners doubt it is worth applying. Khan says 70% of MWBE firms that won contracts benefited from SBS services, and Brewer suggests publicizing that success rate.
chapters.title: Brewer asks how many certified MWBEs actually get city contracts

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And the other thing I hear, but maybe this isn't a statistic that's available.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So you are an MBW Get Certified.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How many of those get city contracts?

utterances.text: My friends are difficult.

utterances.text: They say, oh, Gail, I will apply and I won't get a city contract.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So why do I even apply in the first place?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So is that a number that exists or is it something that just, you know, you don't keep track of?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That is a number that Chief Garner and other principals.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: principles in City Hall are driving agencies to achieve higher utilization.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: On our end.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've been doing that for years, that guy.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Sorry, Hansel.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I missed your question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've been doing that for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So I know they're driving that effort and driving the governance and the policymaking for this program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: What we're really proud of, because we're a resource provider, education agency, and then we do the certification process, is that of the MWB firms that do win contracts, over 70% of them have benefited from SBS services along the way,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: which kind of drives the point that we could be pushing agencies to do more.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We can also be supporting the MWB firms to be best positioned for these contracting opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so we have a robust set of programming that we're always engaged in and always interested in providing support to businesses and putting their best foot forward.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I guess down the line would be making the world know that this number of persons have been certified.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And if you are certified, then X percentage are likely of all of you to get contracts from the city.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So it's worth you putting the time in in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Something to think about.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: To let people know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler

utterances.text: I think it's one at the problem.

utterances.text: That is the problem.

utterances.text: I'm going to just will it into existence.

utterances.text: Stop trying to make fetch stick.

chapters.summary: Stevens says many certified MWBEs, especially Black women and Latinas, are not winning contracts and asks if there are best practices or mentor pairings. She questions whether the city reaches certified firms that have never received an award.
chapters.title: Stevens asks about best practices and mentors for certified firms without contracts

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so, like, as I'm just sitting here and just looking to some of this, and I know you had said that especially you guys are doing a lot of work with the agencies around.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: figuring out how they are like going about doing this.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But like, let's say I'm MWB.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Cause I want to second what council member just said.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I know, I know a number of people who are like, I'm not doing it because that paperwork is just too much.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And then the results just aren't there.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like they just don't match for the effort.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But let's say I am a business.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I do get certified.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, is there a place where I can go where there's like a list of best practices for folks who have already, um,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: who've like gotten contracts and what they've done and like are able to, or can I be like, hey, I need additional help.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Could you pair me with another MWVE to like give me some supports or like some type of mentor?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because it is true.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It is a lot of work to kind of do it for a lot of times, no results.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So just trying to get a better understanding.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Cause again, I'm looking at the numbers and disparities and they look like in, you know, in, in, in groups that already have disparities, there are certain groups that are doing this well.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And a lot of that, a lot of times that's because in that community, they're helping each other.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so are we setting up situations so that like,

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: all folks have places they can go and get the support that they need and trying to figure those things out.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yeah, so that's where we're really proud that 76% of any of all MWB firms that won a contract last year benefited from one of our services.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We really want to encourage every single New York City.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Don't say that because I just have to stop you there.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I say that because, again, we're looking at the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's not saying that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so, like, yes, all of you in the despair, when I'm looking at the numbers, what the chair said.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: There's one in 100 contracts is a Latina or a black woman.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, that's clearly not happening because those folks aren't doing it.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So I'm asking, are there, like, best practices that, like, those folks who are certified in there can go to so that they can start getting those contracts?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because, again, I know it's easy to kind of, like, talk about the board of stuff and be like, oh, we've increased by 10% and we've done this.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That's a lot easy.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But I'm talking about getting down into the disparities and, like, how are we, like, saying, okay.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: This group is doing good in best practices, so do we have best practices that we can share with these groups to make sure that we can start to have diversity in who's getting these contracts?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I know specifically you guys keep talking about the agencies, but I'm talking specifically about the businesses.

chapters.summary: Khan points to the MWBE mentors program, borough events, webinars, and one-on-one technical assistance. He says a large event drew 1,800 attendees and provided over 300 direct one-on-one sessions with more than 60 staff.
chapters.title: Khan describes MWBE mentor program and large outreach events

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So, yes, Councilmember, we have an MWE mentors program that creates space for peer-to-peer mentorship, networking amongst the firms.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So how many of those are done within the specific, and again, and even looking at the Native Americans, they got one contract.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So, like, how are we reaching out to those groups and pairing them with mentors to ensure that they're getting these contracts?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We've done borough-based events.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We've done webinars.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We've done one-on-one technical assistance.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We did two large-scale events, both of which had 1,800 attendees on one end with half of the attendees African-American.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Have you even looked at the list of folks who are like you who've already certified at NWBV and have not gotten a contract and they haven't had a track record and they haven't gotten awarded?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Have you reached out to them specifically and said, you're already certified, let's figure out what's missing so that you can either get.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Get the support that you need to get a contract.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Have you guys done that?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The way in which we get 1,800 to show up under one roof with over 100 services is we reached out to all of the certified firms and said, hey, if you're a certified firm in New York City,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: you should come to this event where we're going to bring all of these resources in one place, do workshops on Passport, do workshops.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We got 1,000 people, and your thought is that in that space and 1,000 people that they're going to get the resources that they need.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We had one-on-one sessions, consultations.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We had workshops at the same event.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We did everything you could possibly think of.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm just trying to, and don't feel like I'm coming at you, but like I'm trying to get to the answer of it because having a big event with a lot of numbers is nice.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I'm saying like, how are we getting to the nitty gritty?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because from that thousand people who showed up, how many people got a contract after that?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So, Councilman, we are not the contracting agency that makes the contracting decisions, right?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But what we did at the event is we provided over 300 direct one-on-one services.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: These are not a large event.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Everybody showed up.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They were sitting and we spoke to them and lectured them.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We had 300 people, one-on-one sessions.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We put all of our staff online.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And it's just one.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: How many staff do you have?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because you had 300 people have direct sessions.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What did that look like?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We had over 60 people working at that event.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: You had 60 staff there, and you met with 300 people.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: How long were those meetings?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Councilmember, we can get you a full briefing on the details of that event, but it's just one event of all of the programs we do year-round.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And the number that I was pointing out earlier, Councilmember, was of any firm that ends up winning a contract in the city, an MWBE firm, of the full fiscal year that we're looking at last fiscal year, FY26,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: it's 76% of them win a contract, which for us demonstrates the need for us to do more, get the word out about these services, get the word out about the program, the mentorship support, the technical assistance.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We help businesses write a capability statement, and we also help them understand the platforms that they use.

chapters.summary: Stevens says if one in 100 contracts goes to Black women or Latinas, the current approach is not working for them. She urges the city to think differently and not burn out women who certify, attend events, and still lose out; Garner agrees and promises better results.
chapters.title: Stevens pushes back that events are not producing contracts for Black and Latina women

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But even if we're saying that the results are still having the disparities that they're having, clearly that's not working.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so if one in every hundred...

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: MWBEs that are getting contracts are black women and Latinas, it's not working for them.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So maybe we should think about other things to do because that's not getting to the people who aren't getting the contracts.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So again, I'm asking the questions because maybe we should think differently, right?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Maybe we should think maybe that thousand event that we had that we can come here and say we had an event where a thousand people showed up is not where the black women or Latino firms are coming to get the information that they need to get certified.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And I know you're about to say, what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: We got 10% this and that.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: What I was going to just say is the majority of the event was black and Latino community members.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So then I guess the numbers that we have aren't real.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So even if they were there, they're still not getting the contracts, correct?

utterances.speaker: Dwight Flynn
utterances.text: And Chief Garner has described the cities.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'll defer to people who are showing up.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Let me speak.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Because then you are having people that are showing up, doing the work, becoming certified, and then still not getting the contracts.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So then what's that going to do is discourage them from actually coming to other things.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yeah, so we are in total agreement with you.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: That we must do a more effective job of not only certifying businesses, but once a business is certified, integrating them at the agency level in the critical path of contracting and procurement.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We hear you.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: We are working internally, overtime.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: In order to increase the city of New York's ability to award contracts in a more broad aspect and focusing on the disparity within the disparity.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Certainly, what the city has done thus far with awarding contracts to black women and Hispanic women and Asian women,

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: is not satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And we are working internally.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And you have my word that these numbers are going to get better.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's not just the word.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I need us to think outside the box and think differently.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So clearly what is being done is not working.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So to tell me you're having events where thousands of people are showing up and they're still not getting contracts, that's not a fix.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And so I hear you like, oh, there was a lot of black women there.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: There was a lot of Latino women there.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That sounds great.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: But if they're showing.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They're certified.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: They're doing all the things that they need to do, and they're still not getting the contract.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: What we're doing isn't working.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And we don't want women, especially women who do extra work all the time, to then get burnt out and say, you know what?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm not doing this anymore.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And that's what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So we have to also speak to that of people wasting their time.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's not easy to be certified, which you all know.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: It's not easy to then have to run a business, to come to these meetings, to have one-on-one consultations and still lose.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Like, that's a lot.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: And that's a lot to ask for.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So what we're doing isn't working.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: So maybe we should change the trajectory and say, okay, that didn't work.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Let's consult and figure out.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Let's go back to the drawing board.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm here to help to have ideas.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I always have ideas.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm not a council member who's just going to sit here and go, why are you doing this?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: I'm saying, what are we going to do?

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: Let's figure it out together because what you're doing isn't working.

utterances.speaker: Althea V. Stevens
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying.

chapters.summary: Restler says progress is real but the city is not doing enough to contract with Black and Latino-owned firms. He calls it a serious inequity and says the committee wants to work together on new engagement ideas and results.
chapters.title: Restler agrees with Stevens on serious inequity in MWBE contracting

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And that is why she's the vice chair of this committee, because she's spot on.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it's right.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The data, you know, I think it's important to recognize progress where it's happened, and we see things moving in a positive direction.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're not doing enough to contract with black and Latino-owned firms, and it's a serious issue.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's a serious inequity.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's one of the core purposes of this program existing and the work that we do in this area, and it's not happening.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's not happening at the scale that it should.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I appreciate the data.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: council members' commitment to kind of say, let's come up with new ideas for engagement.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Let's help get people actually into city contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And, you know, I don't doubt the commitment of the MWB office and the administration.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we really want to see results.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So we're eager to work on this together.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Hopefully we can, you know, some of the things that we've discussed today, I think, can get us there.

chapters.summary: Restler asks about recent changes to the SCA mentorship program and whether the DDC mentorship program continues. Garner says he is unsure about SCA but describes the construction mentoring model from SCA to MTA and a movement toward a race-neutral small business program.
chapters.title: Restler asks Garner about SCA and DDC mentorship program changes

utterances.text: I want to just do a couple of very brief things before we can close out this panel.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know, Chief Garner, you formerly worked at SCA.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I heard that there were recent changes to the mentorship program at the SCA.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Any insight you can offer there?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is the DDC mentorship program continuing or is that discontinued as well?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that a model that was no longer working?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What perspective do you have?

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure about the SCA, but I can tell you that

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: the mentor construction model, which evolved from the SCA to the MTA, in which we, at the MTA, we changed the state law in order to implement that construction mentoring program.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: That model has worked in some very difficult construction organizations.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: There is a movement in implementing.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: a race neutral small business program as we move forward.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler

utterances.text: And so that's who you're speaking to as the extension of your staff?

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Restler says the hearing showed inadequate results for Black and Latino firms, especially Black women and Latinas. He also highlights new subcontracting data efforts and the need to help MWBEs grow from small contracts into larger prime work.
chapters.title: Restler summarizes three takeaways: disparities, subcontracting data, and pipeline

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think I'll just summarize what I think was a good conversation, and I appreciate you all coming today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For me, there are three key takeaways that I really want to focus on moving forward as a committee and working together.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: One is...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are just inadequate results in contracting with black and Latino-owned firms, especially black women and Latina-owned firms, where the numbers are especially abysmal.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Secondly, I'm really excited about the new data you're going to be gathering, and it seems like administration-wide effort to better understand how we're subcontracting, because there may be a good news story to tell there about how we're engaging black and Latino-owned firms that

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: we're not currently seeing once we have a better comprehensive understanding of the subcontracting universe.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And then thirdly is the pipeline, where we've clearly done a...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think, admirable job of engaging more MWBEs in small contracts with the city, but that's not translating into our spend.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so it's still a very small percentage of total spend is going to MWBEs just within the local law 174 framework.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And that has to grow.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really think a deliberate effort to engage the firms that we're working with that are performing well about how do we chart a kind of path forward for them to take on larger contracts

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: is a good priority area for the administration to focus on.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So with that, I'll say thank you very much for coming in today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We really appreciate you taking the time answering questions.

utterances.text: And as Council Lady Gail Brewer and I go back a very long time.

utterances.text: And we were advising the council when James Saunders was in the council.

utterances.text: Oh, I remember.

utterances.speaker: Michael J. Garner
utterances.text: And State Senator James Sanders was one of the— He's championed this legislation to expand the small purchases for MWs, which has really made a difference.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I think he deserves credit.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm not going to say anything about the assembly member who sponsored that bill because I'm not talking nice things about her these days.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But with that, thank you all very much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'll be a laugh.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And appreciate you guys being here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Bring up our next panel in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm not saying anything nice.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: No, I'm going to the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Oh, I got to do.

chapters.summary: Restler opens the hearing to public testimony, reminding attendees to remain silent and that the witness table is reserved for testifiers. He explains that speakers get two minutes, written testimony can be submitted to the Sergeant at Arms or emailed within 72 hours, and audio/video recordings are not accepted.
chapters.title: Restler opens public testimony and gives procedural instructions

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I am now opening the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I would like to remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding, and decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I will try to maintain that myself.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony may...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant of Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant of Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's hearing topic.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant of Arms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimonycouncil.nwc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

chapters.summary: Rana Abdelhamid, founder of Malika and member of the New York Middle Eastern and North African Coalition, supports Intro 208. She says MENA New Yorkers have contributed to the city's business ecosystem but are not counted, and urges codifying MENA inclusion in future disparity studies.
chapters.title: Rana Abdelhamid testifies for Intro 208 and MENA disparity study

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: Good afternoon, council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: Nice to see you as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: Actually, a lot of us are here on behalf of the New York Middle Eastern and North African Coalition, and we're a coalition of organizations across New York State and New York City that represent the needs of North African and Middle Eastern New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: And we're here to support Intro 208.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: So I'll read my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: So my name is Rana Abdul-Hamid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: I'm the founder and executive director of Malika, which is a Queens-based organization that has worked for nearly two decades alongside immigrant, working-class, Muslim, Middle Eastern, and North African New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: I'm also the daughter of Egyptian immigrants born and raised in Queens, and I'm here today to testify in support of Intro 208, in support specifically of a disparity study for the MENA community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: At its core, the disparity study would simply ask the question, who has access to economic opportunities created by our city and who's being left out?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: For many MENA New Yorkers, the problem has been that the city has not even had the data necessary to adequately answer that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: Despite the fact that for generations, Middle Eastern and North African New Yorkers have contributed, you all probably have gone to a deli and met an ak, or had a halal cart food, so you know,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: have contributed to the business ecosystem of the city, we still are not included in many of these studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: We want to make sure that our businesses are...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: counted and that we can measure the number and the realities that impact MENA-owned firms across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: That's why this disparity study matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: This legislation does not ask the council yet to presume what the data will show.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: It just asks the city to collect the data and to look.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: We appreciate already the commitments made from SBS and this current administration to include MENA-owned businesses in the next disparity study,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: but we want to make sure that this is a legal requirement that is codified into the law because we understand that administrations change, commissioners change, priorities change, but the legislation will make sure that our communities are counted despite any changes that might happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: And so today I urge the council to pass Intro 208 to permanently codify the inclusion of Middle Eastern and North African businesses in future disparity studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you, Rana.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really appreciate your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rana Abdelhamid
utterances.text: Good to see you.

chapters.summary: Ikram Arumaim of the Women's Empowerment Coalition of New York City says the organization supports immigrant women and small business owners, including MENA New Yorkers. She says the disparity study would provide data to understand whether disparities exist and how they affect MENA-owned businesses.
chapters.title: Ikram Arumaim testifies for MENA inclusion in disparity studies

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: My name is Ikram Arumaim, and I'm here on behalf of the Women's Empowerment Coalition of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: We See NYC is a community-based organization that supports women and immigrant families through education, workforce development, social services, and other women empowerment programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: Every day, we work with women, immigrant families, and small business owners, including many from the Middle Eastern and North African communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: We see their talent, their hard work, and the contribution they make to New York City's economy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: But we also hear directly from our community about their experiences, the challenges they face when they try to grow their businesses and access opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: That's why this disparity study is so important, and True2Aid would require MENA-owned businesses to be included in future disparity studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: This would provide the data needed to better understand whether disparity exists and where they exist and how they affect businesses in our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: We see NYC stands with our community partners in asking the city to make sure MENA-owned businesses are counted, studied, and visible in this process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: This study is an important opportunity to make sure those experiences are reflected in the data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: When we better understand the disparities

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: our small businesses experience, we can better understand their needs and the opportunities available to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: When our small businesses grow, our families, neighborhoods, and our entire city benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ikram Arumaim
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really appreciate your testimony.

chapters.summary: Bayazir Muhammad Osman of the Muslim Community Network reads testimony from colleague Salah Hashi, a Yemeni American whose father owns a bodega. She says MENA-owned businesses are not separately identified in disparity studies, leaving their barriers and participation invisible.
chapters.title: Bayazir Muhammad Osman shares Yemeni American bodega owner's story

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: Hi everyone, my name is Bayazir Muhammad Osman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: I'm here on behalf of Muslim Community Network.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: We are a New York City-based nonprofit organization that promotes civic engagement, community empowerment, and advocacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: Today I am testifying on behalf of one of my colleagues, Salah Hashi, who isn't able to be with us today, but I wanted to share her story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: This is from her voice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: I'm a Yemeni American, and this issue is personal to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: My father owns a bodega, and growing up, I saw firsthand some of the challenges he faced as a small business owner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: He experienced his barriers related to language, navigating systems, and accessing opportunities that could help his business grow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: Currently, MENA-owned businesses are not separately identified in New York City's disparity studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: Without this information, the city cannot fully understand how MENA businesses are participating in public contracting or whether they face any barriers to opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: This specific, Intro 208, would help address this gap by requiring MENA-owned businesses to be included in future disparity studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: MENA businesses are an important part of the New York City's neighborhoods and economy, as we mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: Small businesses like my father's bodega provide jobs, serve local residents, and become an important part of communities they are located in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: Their experiences should not be overlooked simply because they're not separately represented in the city's data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: I urge the council to pass Intro 208 and ensure MENA-owned businesses are meaningfully included in New York City's disparity analysis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bayazir Muhammad Osman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Habiba Laidi of Malika says MENA-owned businesses are entirely excluded from minority-owned recognition under the MWBE program. She says the city's disparity study failed to separately identify MENA firms, masking barriers and creating a false sense of equity.
chapters.title: Habiba Laidi says MENA firms are lumped in with white-owned businesses

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: My name is Habiba Laidi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: I'm representing Malika.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: The city's MWB program is designed to expand opportunities for historically underrepresented businesses to complete for city contracts and access critical business development resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: Yet right now, Middle Eastern and North African-owned businesses are entirely excluded from being recognized as minority-owned businesses under this program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: This is not an administrative oversight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: It is a profound data failure with economic consequences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: The New York City's most recent disparity study failed to separately identify men-owned businesses, meaning that the city lacks the baseline data necessary to measure their availability, utilization, experience, and discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: Experiences of discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: Instead, the MENA firms are often lumped in with white-owned businesses, benchmarks, and masking systematic barriers and creating a false sense of equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: Across our neighborhoods, inclusion along vibrant commercial corridors like Steinway Street in Astoria, where I'm from, MENA entrepreneurs operate

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: grocery stores, restaurants, pharmacies, retail stores that serve as the heartbeat of our local economy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: Many of these immigrant-owned businesses navigate severe linguistic and cultural barriers, making specialized technical assistance and municipal contracting opportunities

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: through the MWBE program critically necessary for their survival and expansion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: Without these recognitions, our businesses remain invisible and locked out of these tools needed to scale and thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: We are lacking behind other levels of government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: In 2024, the federal government established MENA as a distinct race and ethnicity category, and the New York State subsequently enacted Executive Law 178, which requires

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: state agencies to collect and report data on MENA populations separately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: New York City must align with these crucial progresses that this federal and state government have made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: I strongly urge the council to pass Intro 280.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Habiba Laidi
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Naima Dahir of the Arab American Family Support Center says MENA communities are overlooked despite their contributions. She says MENA-owned businesses may be counted as white, making their challenges invisible, and urges the committee to advance Intro 208 without delay.
chapters.title: Naima Dahir urges passage of Intro 208 for Arab American Family Support Center

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Ressler, Councilmember Stevens, and Councilmember Brewer, and members of the Committee on Contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: My name is Naima Dahir, and I'm the Advocacy Manager at the Arab American Family Support Center, also known as AAFSC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: AAFSC serves over 20,000 New Yorkers each year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Our staff speak more than 20 different languages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Over 70% of our clients were born outside of the United States, many from historically underserved communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Our work centers on families by helping them stabilize during challenging times, maintain stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: And ultimately thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: This includes uplifting economic empowerment and making sure our communities have the opportunities to thrive in New York City, including through small business ownership and economic support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Middle Eastern and North African communities have been long overlooked despite their contributions to the culture and makeup of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: MENA-owned businesses are staples in our communities and are well-loved by the people they serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: These businesses go through many of the same hurdles associated with small business ownership, but are currently not recognized as minority-owned businesses under New York City's MWBE program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: This classification has significant consequences for our communities and highlights an unfair gap in the city's economic opportunity programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: New York City's most recent disparity study did not look at MENA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: to own businesses separately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Because of this, the city does not have enough information to know how many MENA businesses are competing for city contracts, how often they receive these contracts, how much funding they receive, or whether they face discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Instead, MENA-owned businesses may be counted as white businesses, which makes their particular and unique experiences and challenges invisible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: We have seen the real impact of these disparities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, when businesses were receiving rent relief and other support, Arab-owned businesses were often left out or had difficulty accessing these resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: This shows why it's important for MENA-owned businesses to properly be identified and included in the data the city uses to make decisions about economic opportunities and support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Intro 208, sponsored by Councilmember Shahana Hanif, would require MENA-owned businesses to be included in future disparity studies used to determine eligibility for the program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: This is a critical first step towards greater inclusion of MENA-owned businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: We urge the committee to advance Intro 208 and the full City Council to pass it without delays.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: MENA-owned businesses have contributed to New York City's economy for generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: They should no longer be invisible in data that determines the economic opportunities and the supports that they need to succeed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Naima Dahir
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Restler quotes Mike Bloomberg, saying in God we trust and everyone else bring the data. He says without data on MENA businesses the city cannot structure the right policies, and thanks Council Member Hanif for pushing Intro 208.
chapters.title: Restler thanks MENA panel and supports data-driven policy

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really want to thank this whole panel for coming and for your thoughtful testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: My favorite Mike Bloomberg quote is always, in God we trust, everyone else bring the data.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it's so true.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: If we don't have the data to understand the demographics of the MENA community, the businesses in the MENA community, then we can't structure the right policies to support that community.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And as the council member who represents Atlantic Avenue and downtown Brooklyn and Borum Hill, like many of the, you know, there are just extraordinary, extraordinary MENA businesses that have been,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: that have called our community home for 100 years and have done so much to make our community the special place that it is.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really am grateful to Councilmember Hanif for pushing this legislation, and I'm happy that we have the opportunity to have a hearing on it today and look forward to working together with all of you on the next steps.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Unless either of you have questions.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Appreciate you all being here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.
