chapters.summary: Matt Gove says the Surfrider Foundation appreciates Council Member Epstein's bill to reduce single-use cups. He warns that replacing them with compostable cups is a false solution and says reusable or thin aluminum cups are better options.
chapters.title: Matt Gove of Surfrider Foundation supports Intro 896 but opposes compostable loophole

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm here for the bill about reusable and single-use cups that's on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Go for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: Oh, we're doing it all right now.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This is your chance to give your three minutes of glory.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: Well, I thank you all for hearing this bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: And sorry, I lost track of what was going on with the first issue on the agenda that was going on for the last two hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: I'm Matt Gove from the Surfrider Foundation, and we appreciate Councilmember Epstein's bill to try to reduce single-use cups used by city government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: I think everyone knows now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: How much damage plastic has to human health, and also how much garbage it creates, and the city has to pay to get rid of that garbage, and when that garbage is burned, it releases lots of pollutants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: So we thank you for the bill, and I've heard there are rumors that the text may change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: We're very concerned with the text.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: Where it says the city can just

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: replace those single-use cups with compostable cups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: Compostable sounds good, but it's one of those rabbit holes that you go down and then you are not wanting to use one of these compostable cups because they're just as bad, sometimes even worse than just a regular throwaway cup.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: So we're hoping that'll be taken out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: Really, the only option is a reusable cup, or if you have to, there's those very thin aluminum cups that can be reused or easily recycled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: So sadly for cups, there's not a lot of options, but reusable always works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Gove
utterances.text: So we thank you for this bill and thanks for the time to testify.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Matt.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We really appreciate your thoughtful testimony in support of Councilmember Epstein's legislation around compostable cups.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we're really happy to have the chance to have a hearing on it today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We'll now go to Ms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Eve Fox.

chapters.summary: Eve Fox, director at the Story of Stuff Project, says the bill's compostable exemption undermines its goals. She argues compostable bioplastics contain toxic additives like PFAS, have heavy climate footprints, and require industrial composting infrastructure that many communities lack.
chapters.title: Eve Fox of Story of Stuff warns compostable cups are still plastic

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Hi, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: My name is Eve Fox.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: I'm the Director of Development and Marketing at the Story of Stuff Project, a nonprofit dedicated to waste reduction and sustainability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Prior to that, I served on the leadership team at Beyond Plastics, a nonprofit led by Judith Ankh, former U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: EPA Region 2 administrator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: And while I applaud the intent of the bill, I agree with Matt, it contains a critical loophole that threatens to undermine its goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Exempting compostable single-use cups creates a false solution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Replacing conventional plastic cups with bioplastic or compostable alternatives fails to protect public health and the environment for four main reasons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: One, they're still plastic and therefore pose serious health risks because even compostable plastic cups are often made entirely of bio-based plastics like PLA or those that look paper are often lined with a hidden plastic film.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Bioplastics are manufactured using the same chemical processing methods as traditional plastics and frequently contain toxic chemical additives, including PFAS, that are used to make them more resistant to water and grease.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: In fact, a peer-reviewed April 2025 study in food safety and toxicology revealed that exposure to starch-based microplastics resulted in liver and intestinal lesions, elevated blood sugars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: It messed with lipid metabolism and disrupted gut microbiota, leading the authors to urge strict evaluation of bioplastic safety before use in food packaging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: So-called compostable plastics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Crop crops also have a heavy climate footprint and use a ton of resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: They are not carbon neutral.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Growing these crops to produce them takes up a lot of land, water, and fossil fuel inputs and takes farmland away from actual food production.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Furthermore, when compostable packaging, which includes cups, inevitably ends up in a landfill due to a lack of industrial processing,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: it breaks down anaerobically and releases methane, which is a greenhouse gas that's roughly 30 times more potent than carbon dioxide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: There is the elephant in the room with all things compostable that are beyond green waste is that there's a lack of industrial composting processing and infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Certified compostable plastics don't break down in backyard compost bins or a natural environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: They require high heat industrial composting facilities that have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: precise control over temperature, moisture, and oxygen, which is something that many communities lack the access to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: And even when they do make it into composting systems, there is a widespread facility rejection due to system contamination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Municipal and commercial composters increasingly refuse to accept compostable foodware, such as cups, because these products introduce toxic chemicals that may include PFAS into their finished compost and they create severe

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: consumer confusion, which leads to even more widespread contamination from conventional plastics that are mixed into the composting stream.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Major compost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Listing operators, including those serving the state of Oregon and commercial facilities across California, now explicitly request keeping bioplastics out of the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Time expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eve Fox
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Fox.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That was really insightful testimony, and we really appreciate you taking the time to share your expertise with us around compostable cups and the importance of tailoring this legislation correctly.

chapters.summary: Vicki Abu-Ghallous of the Story of Stuff Project and Reusable New York City Coalition says the city spends $1.7 billion annually on garbage collection, with $381 million from packaging waste. She recommends removing compostable language and adding reusable cup systems and water refill stations.
chapters.title: Vicki Abu-Ghallous urges banning all single-use cups and promoting reuse

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We will now go to Vicky Abdu-Galium and Ms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And ma'am, I apologize if I've mispronounced your name.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You have three minutes if you'd like to testify, starting now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: Chair Ressler, members of the Committee on Contracts, my name is Vicki Abugallium, and I'm delivering my testimony today on behalf of the Story of Stuff Project and as a member organization of the Reusable New York City Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: The story of stuff, as my colleague shared, is a nonprofit organization advocating for solutions to the plastic waste crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: And one of our main focus areas for addressing the plastic waste crisis is through reuse as a solution to plastic pollution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: As was already shared in other testimony, we know we're drowning in disposables.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: Each year, the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: Food service industry purchases nearly 11 trillion disposable items, which equates to a $24 billion spend on products that are used for literal minutes and then thrown away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: In New York City alone, the cost of collecting garbage for disposal surpasses $1.7 billion annually, with $381 million of those dollars due to packaging waste, most of which is food packaging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: So we're really excited to see the council considering a bill that aims to reduce plastic pollution generated by agencies through banning single-use plastic cups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: But I echo the concerns of the others providing testimony with Intro 896 has a major flaw.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: Allowing single-use compostable cups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: for the same reasons that were already stated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: And so I'll make the most use of my time by saying that I agree with the concerns shared by others on the toxicity of compostables and the inability of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: our current systems to really even handle them and generate quality compost product.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: And focus my testimony on reuse as a solution to that issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: As a leading advocate in single-use plastic waste

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: pollution and reusable solutions, we are seeing municipalities all across the country struggle to source compostables and enforce a switch from plastic to bioplastic and so-called compostables.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: So it's our position that if the goal is to reduce single-use disposables, why not ban all types of single-use cups?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: In my written testimony that I submitted, I recommended some changes to the bill text.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: Namely removing the language about compostables being acceptable, and then also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: implementing language that encourages the use of reusable beverage bottles when possible and the implementation of accessible water bottle refill stations per 500 occupants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: Authorized under a building's maximum capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: And additional text changes that the council might consider that are regarding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: reusable beverage cup reuse systems being implemented in agency offices, buildings, or indoor facilities, and on agency property, as well as prohibiting the distribution of beverages in disposable beverage cups on those properties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: Time expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: Zero waste hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: Focuses on reduce and reuse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: Thank you for considering my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vicki Abu-Ghallous
utterances.text: We really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you for the thoughtful testimony and for providing feedback on the legislation that we will be sure to share with the bill sponsor, Councilmember Epstein.

chapters.summary: Jacob Yatsiliel says the Association of Black Contractors' report calls MWBE the mechanism of disenfranchisement for small Black women-owned businesses. He calls for oversight hearings to include affected small women-owned businesses and says the system must be reformed or taxpayer funding should stop.
chapters.title: Jacob Yatsiliel of Association of Black Contractors calls for MWBE system reform

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We will now ask Jacob Yatsiliel to testify as well.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You have three minutes beginning now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We can hear you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: Okay, thanks for having this meeting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: And I do want to agree with the chairman, Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: There's not too many good things that can be said about the Adams administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: I want to make a suggestion that these hearings are probably more fruitful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: If you were actually to include testimony from small women-owned businesses with equal time as the people who have been appointed by the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: The Association of Black Contractors, I'm the chair of the Association of Black Contractors, and we issue regular reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: And our latest report,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: entitled MWBE, the mechanism of disenfranchisement that was forwarded to your office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: And it was given that title because the policies, practices, and procedures of New York City dismantles small Black women-owned businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: Now, the Association of Black Contractors

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: We have submitted legislative proposals and the system that we're currently under, it needs to be reformed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: And if it's not reformed, we're just moving chairs around and nothing is being accomplished.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: If the system is not reformed, we would push for...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: The taxpayer to be freed from the burden of funding these failed programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: When you look at our data, which we regularly issue reports, you look at our data combined with the controller's report, and I do believe the controller's data is correct,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: you will come to the conclusion that the chair's hunch is correct, that these agencies do not care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: So we're calling for oversight hearings to include testimony from the affected parties, which are the small women-owned businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jacob Yatsiliel
utterances.text: And we welcome the opportunity to work with Chairman Ressler's office to bring about these legislative proposals.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really want to thank you for your testimony, and we would love to engage further with the Association of Black Contractors and yourself and appreciate the feedback on our hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I share your sentiments.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I feel like we would have been better served by more participation from...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: MWBE firms and associations that advocate for those firms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And in future MWB oversight hearings, we'll do a better job of making sure that those folks are properly engaged and participating.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you, and we very much look forward to following up.

chapters.summary: Tanisha Hurd of the Bronx Chamber of Commerce says the chamber supports Intro 694's expanded outreach when MWBE targets are unmet and Intro 208's inclusion of MENA entrepreneurs. She says MENA communities are growing in the Bronx and should be studied for MWBE eligibility and access. Restler thanks her and adjourns the hearing.
chapters.title: Tanisha Hurd of Bronx Chamber of Commerce supports Intro 694 and 208

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And the last person slated to testify today doesn't share their name, so we'll have to ask you to share your name on the record.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we have you listed as the new BXCC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Ressler and members of the Committee on Contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: My name is Tanisha Hurd, and I'm representing the Bronx Chamber of Commerce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: The Bronx Chamber is really critical in helping local businesses in the Bronx grow, thrive, and remain competitive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: And for many Bronx entrepreneurs, especially first-gen business owners, the chamber is the very first place they turn to for support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: And so the Bronx Chamber fully supports Intro 694, which would expand government outreach when MWBE utilization targets are unmet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: And intro.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: 208, which will include Middle Eastern and North African entrepreneurs in getting NWBE certifications.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: In the Bronx, the Middle Eastern and North African community is a vital and growing part of our borough, home to cultural centers like Little Yemen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: Nationwide, we've seen how Middle Eastern and North African Americans are underrepresented in government data, which is suppressing the economic needs of this group and preventing them from accessing programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: To build on the great work MWBE is doing, we would assess Middle Eastern and North African Americans for program eligibility, especially as our community continues to grow here in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: As it relates to Intro 694, where it will study business owners within this group through disparity studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: If the results show that they are eligible, the program will include them in the MWBE benefits and continue supporting the growth for Bronx businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: Alongside adding new business owners, the MWBE program must also strengthen mechanisms to improve equity in the Bronx by implementing Intro 208.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: By requiring government agencies to conduct education and outreach if they do not reach their goals, businesses under MWBE

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: will have improved access to contracts and opportunities, and their success will expand through the borough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: Expanding access to MWBE programs and strengthening its requirements will help ensure more city dollars reach Bronx businesses and communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: By investing in our diverse businesses, we strengthen our local economy, our borough, and of course, the city at large.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: So we look forward to working with the council to continue to strengthen local businesses and the chamber fully supports Intro 208 and 964.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: And we hope that you are able to move these critical bills forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Hurd, and we really appreciate you taking the time to testify and look forward to working with the New Bronx Chamber of Commerce.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that they're definitely an important partner for SBS as we do more to engage more MWBEs and get them connected to city contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that that is all we have for today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So with that, I just want to thank everybody for coming.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Ashley, thank you for spending however many hours with us and everybody else for being here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We appreciate you, and I hope everybody has a wonderful afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We're adjourned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tanisha Hurd
utterances.text: Take care.

summary: Committee on Contracts held an oversight hearing on M/WBE utilization in city contracts, with testimony from Chief Business Diversity Officer Michael Garner, MOCS, and SBS.
Council members pressed the administration on stagnant MWBE contract value, severe disparities for Black, Latino, and women-owned firms, and missing subcontracting data.

Public witnesses testified in support of Intro 208 adding MENA-owned businesses to disparity studies and Intro 896 restricting single-use cups, with several speakers opposing a compostable-cup loophole.
